title: Decision gates
blurb: State the purpose of decision gates: governance checkpoints between phases where the sponsor or board decides whether to continue.
question: At the end of the definition phase of a hospital car park project, updated estimates show costs have risen sharply and forecast demand has fallen. The governance board meets before any construction money is committed. What is the purpose of this meeting, and what could it decide?

teach.body: Decision gates are points between the phases of a life cycle where the continuation of the project is decided. The sponsor or governance board reviews the business case, the progress made and the readiness for the next phase, then decides: go, no-go, hold or re-plan. In plain English: before committing more money and effort, the people accountable stop and ask, 'Is this still worth doing, and are we ready for the next step?'

teach.h: Gates in a linear life cycle
teach.caption: Each phase ends at a gate. Nobody moves into the next phase until the decision has been made.

teach.body: Three questions. Is the business case still valid: do the benefits still justify the costs and risks? How did the phase just finished go: were its outputs delivered and is progress acceptable? Is the project ready for the next phase: are plans, funding and resources in place? Because the business case is rechecked at every gate, a project that has stopped being worthwhile can be caught early.

root.label: Decision gate
root.sub: decided by the sponsor or governance board

children.label: Re-plan
children.sub: revise plans or case, then return

teach.h: Worked scenario: the hospital car park
teach.body: Midshire Hospital plans a multi-storey car park. At the definition gate, the board sees that estimates have risen sharply and forecast demand has fallen, because more staff now travel by bus. The business case no longer stacks up. Instead of letting construction start, the board decides to re-plan: a smaller design is prepared and brought back to the gate, where it gets a 'go'. Without the gate, the full-size car park would have been built at a loss.

teach.h: Who does what at a gate
head: Role
At the gate
rows: Makes the go, no-go, hold or re-plan decision
Presents progress, plans for the next phase, risks
Reviewed: is the project still justified?
May support with reporting and assurance

teach.text: The project manager does NOT make the gate decision: the sponsor or governance board does. A gate is not automatic progress, it is not a lessons-learned session (that is a post-project review) and it is not an inspection of outputs (that is quality control). It is a governance decision about whether to continue.

items: Decision gates: points between phases where the continuation of the project is decided.
The sponsor or governance board decides: go, no-go, hold or re-plan.
They review the business case, progress so far and readiness for the next phase.
Purpose: governance control, committing resources phase by phase and stopping unviable projects early.

summary: You can now state the purpose of decision gates: governance checkpoints between phases where the sponsor or board reviews the business case, progress and readiness and decides to go, stop, hold or re-plan. You can also explain why stopping an unviable project early is a success, not a failure.

A.q: Why does a project pause at a decision gate between phases?
options: To capture lessons for future projects
To decide whether the project continues
To test outputs against their criteria
To check benefits after the project ends
A.why: A decision gate is where the sponsor or governance board decides whether the project should continue into the next phase.

whyNot.0: Capturing lessons for future projects is the purpose of a post-project review.
whyNot.2: Testing outputs against criteria is quality control.
whyNot.3: Checking benefits after the project ends is a benefits review.

A.q: Where are decision gates positioned in a linear life cycle?
A.why: Decision gates sit between the phases, so continuation is decided before each new phase begins.

whyNot.1: Gates occur throughout the life cycle, not just at the start.
whyNot.2: After closure there is no further phase to decide on.
whyNot.3: Work packages are units of work, not points where the project's continuation is decided.

A.q: Who normally makes the decision at a decision gate?
A.why: The sponsor or governance board makes the gate decision; the project manager provides the information.

whyNot.0: The project manager prepares the evidence but does not decide whether the project continues.
whyNot.1: The team does the work; it does not make governance decisions.
whyNot.2: An auditor may give assurance, but does not decide whether the project continues.

B.q: Which of the following is NOT a typical outcome of a decision gate?
B.why: Gates decide go, no-go, hold or re-plan. Changes to the baseline go through change control, not blanket approval at a gate.

whyNot.0: Proceeding (go) is a normal gate outcome.
whyNot.1: Holding until conditions are met is a normal gate outcome.
whyNot.3: Stopping (no-go) is a normal gate outcome.

B.q: At the end of definition, a governance board finds that costs have risen sharply and expected benefits have fallen. Which gate outcome would best protect the organisation?
options: Stop or re-plan, as the case is weak
Proceed, but skip the next gate
Let the project manager decide alone
B.why: When the business case no longer justifies the project, the board should stop it or re-plan before committing more resources.

whyNot.0: Finishing a phase does not mean the project is still worth continuing.
whyNot.2: Skipping gates removes governance control just when it is most needed.
whyNot.3: The gate decision belongs to the sponsor or board, not the project manager.

B.q:
Which THREE of the following are typically considered at a decision gate?
1. Whether the business case is still valid
2. Progress in the phase just completed
3. Readiness for the next phase
4. Whether benefits have been realised after closure
B.why: A gate reviews the business case, progress so far and readiness for the next phase.

whyNot.1: Statement 4 is wrong: benefits after closure are checked in a benefits review.
whyNot.2: Statement 4 is wrong, and progress in the phase just completed (2) is a key input.
whyNot.3: Statement 4 is wrong, and the business case (1) is central to every gate.

C.q: Why is it valuable that a decision gate can stop a project?
options: It guarantees the project will finish early
It removes the need for a business case
It lets the team skip quality control
It stops unviable work before more is spent
C.why: Gates let the organisation stop a project that is no longer viable before committing further money and effort.

whyNot.0: Gates give control over continuation; they do not guarantee an early finish.
whyNot.1: The business case is what the gate reviews, so it is still needed.
whyNot.2: Quality control is still needed; gates do not replace it.

C.q: A project manager tells the team: 'Definition is finished, so we start deployment on Monday.' No review has been held. Which governance control has been bypassed?
C.why: Moving into a new phase should follow a decision gate, where the sponsor or board decides whether to continue.

whyNot.0: A post-project review happens at or after closure, not between phases.
whyNot.1: A benefits review checks benefits, usually after the project has closed.
whyNot.3: An audit checks compliance; it does not authorise moving into the next phase.

C.q: How does a decision gate differ from a post-project review?
options: A gate decides on continuing; a review captures lessons
A gate captures lessons; a review decides on continuing
Both are held only after the project has closed
A gate measures benefits; a review checks compliance
C.why: A decision gate decides whether to continue to the next phase; a post-project review evaluates how the project was managed and captures lessons.

whyNot.2: Gates are held between phases during the project, not after closure.
whyNot.3: Measuring benefits is a benefits review and checking compliance is an audit.

reteach.title: Think of buying a house
reteach.question: Buying a house happens in stages, and at several points you decide whether to carry on. How is that like a project's decision gates?

blocks.body: After viewing, you decide whether to make an offer. After the survey, you decide whether to proceed, renegotiate the price, or walk away because of subsidence. Before exchanging contracts, you check the mortgage is in place. At each point you ask: is it still worth it, and am I ready for the next step? Walking away after a bad survey is not failure: it saves you from a far costlier mistake. That is exactly what a decision gate does.

blocks.text: You, the buyer (the sponsor), make the decision at each gate, not the estate agent doing the legwork (the project manager).

explain.body: Decision gates sit at the end of each phase, before the next one starts, so no new phase begins without a decision.

test.q: Complete the statement: decision gates are points ______ where the continuation of the project is decided.
test.why: Decision gates are points between phases where the continuation of the project is decided.

whyNot.0: Tasks are managed day to day; gates decide on whole phases.
whyNot.1: After closure there is nothing left to continue.
whyNot.2: Gates are formal governance points, not part of every meeting.

explain.h: The business case at the centre
explain.body: At every gate the business case is reviewed: do the expected benefits still justify the costs and risks? Progress and readiness for the next phase are checked too.

test.q: Which document is most central to the go or no-go decision at a gate?
test.why: The business case justifies the project, so gates review whether it is still valid before continuing.

whyNot.0: Lessons may inform plans, but the justification for continuing is in the business case.
whyNot.2: Test scripts support quality control of outputs, not the continuation decision.
whyNot.3: Configuration records track items and versions, not whether the project is still justified.

explain.body: Go: proceed. Hold: pause until conditions are met. Re-plan: revise and come back. No-go: stop the project.

test.q: A board decides the project may continue only once funding for the next phase is confirmed, and pauses it until then. Which gate outcome is this?
test.why: Pausing until a condition is met is a 'hold' decision.

whyNot.0: Go would let the project proceed now, without waiting.
whyNot.1: No-go would stop the project rather than pause it.
whyNot.3: Handover is part of transition, not a gate decision.

explain.body: Gates give the sponsor and governance board control: resources are committed one phase at a time, and unviable projects can be stopped early.

test.q: Which of the following statements about a decision gate is accurate?
options: The project manager alone makes the gate decision
They are a governance control on continuation
They are only held at the end of a project
They replace the need for a business case
test.why: Decision gates are a governance control: the sponsor or board decides whether the project continues.

whyNot.0: The sponsor or governance board decides, not the project manager.
whyNot.2: Gates are held between phases throughout the life cycle.
whyNot.3: Gates review the business case; they do not replace it.
